scope: Grade XI Unit 7 Topic 7.1 — consolidated 80-source-item teacher decision queue

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF lists crystalline, polycrystalline and amorphous classes. It also parenthetically equates polycrystalline with polymeric, which is NOT a general scientific synonym; polycrystalline describes grains and polymeric describes macromolecular composition.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Explain polycrystalline grain structure versus polymer macromolecules; do not teach textbook shorthand as scientific synonym

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF explicitly describes crystalline solids as having regular, well-defined particle arrangement. The authored explanation matches this core definition.
NBF defines polycrystalline as many small crystals or grains with different orientations. This should not be conflated with the chain structure of a polymer.
NBF describes disordered amorphous/glassy arrangement, with possible short-range ordered pockets. Avoid saying no ordering exists at any scale.
The passage explicitly defines amorphous as without regular form or structure. The question primarily checks terminology recall.
NBF calls a unit cell the smallest basic portion of a crystal repeatedly stacked in three dimensions. The authored explanation is consistent.
The chapter distinguishes the repeating unit from the extended crystal lattice; the original key/explanation pair fits the terminology.
Monomer is correct scientific vocabulary for repeated building units but is not explicitly introduced by name in the printed NBF polymer paragraph.
entries.optionalQualitySuggestion: Monomer terminology is supplementary to NBF 'small molecules'

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF explicitly names polymerization as the process forming long chains. The source explanation uses 'monomers', an accurate term outside the paragraph's exact wording.
entries.optionalQualitySuggestion: Align original explanation to the passage's 'small molecules' wording

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: Original intended choice remains source-supported and V149 replaced an off-passage distractor. The ORIGINAL one-line explanation falsely says nylon is listed among this paragraph's synthetic examples; rewrite the explanation using printed examples.
NBF names PVC as a synthetic polymer. The author's answer/explanation pairing is source-consistent at first pass.
NBF identifies X-ray diffraction for studying atomic arrangement of crystals. This is an instrument-method recall fact rather than direct B22 structural comparison.
NBF explicitly includes constituent atoms, ions or molecules in crystalline materials. Original explanation supports the choice.
NBF's Figure 7.1 illustrates the NaCl ionic crystal. This example recognition alone does not establish B22 Understanding-level discrimination.
V149 carries V147's narrower wording because NBF lists sulphur as a crystalline nonmetal, not explicitly as a molecular crystalline category in this passage. Teacher must approve that change.
NBF calls small crystals in a polycrystalline sample crystallites or grains. The authored explanation agrees with this definition.

NBF describes direction-dependent measurements for crystals. It is reasonable at this course level but particular properties/symmetries can show exceptions; avoid teaching an all-properties universal rule.
NBF describes polycrystalline materials as isotropic in its idealized treatment; for a real polycrystal this is commonly approximate when grains are randomly oriented.
NBF Figure 7.5(c) and Figure 7.6 use three edges and angles to characterize cell geometry. This is supporting crystallography rather than full B22 classification.
Figure 7.5(b) shows the three named cubic unit-cell forms. The MCQ is identification/recall, not direct comparison of different solid classes.
NBF p.113 links a crystal's regular structure to anisotropic behavior. The authored reason is scientifically sound; particular measured properties depend on symmetry and direction.
NBF p.113 treats randomly oriented grains as isotropic. The question responsibly says 'approximately' and the keyed explanation attributes averaging to differently oriented crystallites.

The distinction between one continuous ordered crystal and a polycrystal containing multiple oriented grains is supported by NBF p.113. Real crystals may still contain defects, so 'continuous order' is an idealization.
NBF p.114 identifies glass with amorphous solids and shows lack of a repeating long-range atomic arrangement. Avoid describing glass as gas or a perfect single crystal.
NBF p.114 explicitly mentions local ordered pockets in an amorphous sample despite widespread disorder. The question distinguishes local order from long-range periodic order.

NBF p.115 describes unit-cell repetition forming the crystal lattice. For scientific precision, a mathematical lattice is periodic points while the full crystal structure also includes a basis; the question uses the NBF's simplified description.
entries.optionalQualitySuggestion: Lattice as periodic sites versus crystal structure with basis: optional advanced clarification

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF p.115 says stacking a unit cell repeatedly in three dimensions generates the crystal structure. The answer concept is consistent with this description.
NBF p.113 names salts, metals, nonmetals and ionic compounds as crystalline examples. The intended statement that distinct substances can have different structures is supported.
Figure 7.4 and p.113 distinguish ordered grains from amorphous disorder. Random grain orientation does not remove local periodicity within a crystallite.

NBF p.113 states that polycrystalline solids contain many small crystals or grains; the printed parenthetical use of 'polymeric' is scientifically nonstandard. Teacher must explicitly distinguish polycrystalline grains from polymer-chain molecules.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Explicitly distinguish polycrystalline (grains) from polymeric (chain molecules)

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF p.114 says repeated small molecules make long chains by polymerization. The explanation's 'monomer' vocabulary is scientifically correct but not explicitly introduced on this printed page.
entries.optionalQualitySuggestion: Original explanation's monomer terminology is outside the printed NBF term

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF p.114 contrasts naturally occurring polymers (rubber, resin, wood) with synthetic examples (polythene, polystyrene, PVC). Both are chain polymers; the origin distinction is supported.

NBF p.114 explains amorphous disorder; the answer prudently states that lacking periodicity MAY indicate amorphous structure. Phrase 'sharp long-range lattice pattern' could be rewritten as 'regular long-range repeating atomic arrangement' to avoid ambiguous diffraction connotations.
entries.optionalQualitySuggestion: Optionally replace ambiguous 'lattice pattern' with long-range repeating atomic arrangement

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF p.113 directly defines crystallites/grains. Although V148 provisionally labelled Understanding, the present stem largely tests retrieval of a definition. It strongly overlaps earlier grain-definition items.
NBF p.113 identifies X-ray diffraction and p.115 repeats it in structure study. The intended reason connects diffraction to periodic order; avoid frequent repetition with Q12 in the same quiz.
NBF p.113 shows the ionic NaCl crystal in Figure 7.1. A repeating ionic arrangement with metal cations is consistent with an ionic crystalline material.
NBF p.115 explicitly defines unit cell as a basic repeating portion. Despite V148's provisional Understanding label, the item is essentially a definition-identification question.

NBF p.114 classifies glass as amorphous with lack of regular structure. The physical solid form does not require long-range crystalline periodicity; avoid presenting the outdated 'liquid' shorthand as literal.
NBF p.113 illustrates sodium-chloride crystalline order, while p.114 lists amorphous glass; contrast of these materials is well grounded.
The NBF p.113 unit introduction expressly links atomic order/bonding to properties and material choice. The original explanation stays within this general claim.

Figure 7.5(b) places positions at the eight cube corners. Eight corner positions are not eight independent effective atoms: eight corner contributions of one-eighth give one net lattice atom per conventional SC cell.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Distinguish eight drawn SC corner sites from one effective atom per conventional unit cell

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: The BCC sketch adds a body-centre position to corner positions. It is a cubic lattice distinction; explanation should not imply the eight corner positions cease to exist.

Figure 7.5(b) has corners and six face-centre sites for FCC. They are geometrical positions; shared face-centred contributions produce three effective atoms plus one from corners, for four effective sites.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Distinguish FCC face positions from effective cell contents (four atoms)

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: BCC is the cubic form with a lattice position at the body centre, as shown in Figure 7.5(b). This duplicates the central distinction in Q42 and Q59.
A cube has six faces and the conventional FCC diagram marks each face centre. Six geometrical marked positions do not equal six unshared cell atoms; total effective FCC contents are four atoms.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Six FCC face positions are not six unshared atoms

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: Figure 7.6 sets a=b=c for the cubic system. The same fundamental edge relation is tested again explicitly in Q48.
Figure 7.6 identifies alpha=beta=gamma=90 degrees for the cubic case. Q49 tests the same relation in symbolic form.
The relation a=b=c comes from the cubic unit-cell diagram in Figure 7.6. It repeats the scientific concept in Q46 with symbolic wording.
The alpha=beta=gamma=90-degree relation is shown for the cubic system. Q47 measures the same requirement in prose.

The source differentiates seven crystal systems through relationships among edge lengths and interaxial angles. Although mapped to Understanding_candidate in V148, the existing stem may be retrieval of the classification criterion rather than demonstrating discrimination.
Figure 7.6 includes hexagonal among seven systems. This is a textbook figure recognition fact, not an Understanding-level comparison of crystalline/amorphous/polymeric structures.
Figure 7.6 illustrates seven distinct crystal systems; it does not indicate seven cubic structures. Reinforce that SC/BCC/FCC are cubic lattice arrangements, not the seven crystal systems themselves.

The three pictured cubic arrangements differ in the locations of lattice sites: cube corners only, centre, or faces. Wording is source-consistent and broadly conceptual, but it is supporting crystallography rather than direct P-11-B-22 classification.

Figure 7.5(a) illustrates a repeating unit cell. The prompt largely identifies a definition already studied in Q6/Q37; V148 provisional Understanding label merits lowering to Recall pending teacher review.
NBF pp.113 and 115 connect periodic atomic order with crystalline solids. This is the batch's strongest direct link to distinguishing structural classes under B-22.

Figure 7.5(b) shows one geometrical centre position in the BCC conventional cell. The effective BCC count is two atoms per cell including shared corner sites; the question does not ask for total atoms.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: One BCC body-centre position, two effective atoms total

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: Six face-centre positions are pictured in FCC, but each face is shared by two adjacent cells. NBF p.115 gives four effective atoms per FCC cell; explain the distinction explicitly.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Six FCC face positions, four effective atoms in conventional unit cell

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: Corners without face/body positions describe the textbook SC arrangement. This is a word-described recognition task, not an actual shared-stimulus image item; nearly duplicates Q41.
Corner positions with one central body site give a conventional BCC diagram. This repeats the feature examined in Q42/Q44/Q56.
Corner positions with face-centre sites give FCC, source Figure 7.5(b). This tests the same fundamental relation as Q43/Q45/Q57.
NBF p.113 illustrates NaCl with regular ionic order. The original choice points to crystalline solid, but unrelated gas/liquid distractors make this very easy despite a student scenario.

V147's source-aligned stem replaces the original misleading 'random long-range arrangement' with no regular long-range repeating arrangement. The key option remains compatible; teacher must formally approve the changed stem.
NBF p.113 defines polycrystals from many smaller ordered grains with different orientations. This does not mean polymer chains are the same scientific concept as polycrystalline grains.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Polycrystalline grains do not mean polymer chains

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: Figure 7.5(b) shows BCC cube corners plus one central position. The situation describes rather than displays a visual model, so it is a standalone recognition item rather than verified grouped stimulus.
Figure 7.5(b) shows conventional FCC corners and sites at all six face centres. Six geometrical face sites are shared between cells and do not mean six whole face atoms counted in one cell.
NBF p.113 describes crystallographic direction dependence. The observed difference between two crystal directions supports anisotropy, although weak unrelated distractors limit difficulty.
NBF p.113 idealizes bulk polycrystal isotropy. 'Approximately' is scientifically defensible for many randomly oriented grains; no implication that each grain itself is isotropic.
NBF p.114 explicitly calls long-chain formation polymerization. The original one-line explanation says monomers, which is valid supplementary terminology but not named in this paragraph.
entries.optionalQualitySuggestion: Optional monomer vocabulary alignment with textbook

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF p.114 lists polyvinyl chloride among synthetic polymers. A material's polymer identity and its degree of amorphous/crystalline order describe different aspects and are not exclusive categories.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Polymer composition and crystalline/amorphous order are independent descriptors

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: The NBF names rubber as naturally occurring polymer, and also lists rubber under amorphous solid examples. Both can be true: chemical composition/origin and atomic order are distinct axes.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Rubber may be both natural polymer and amorphous

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: Figure 7.6 has a=b=c and all right interaxial angles for cubic cells. This is useful supporting structure identification, not direct classification of glass versus polymer.
The NBF distinguishes regular long-range order in crystals from amorphous glass, which can retain local short-range arrangements. A real structure-comparison scenario closer to P-11-B-22.
NBF p.115 calls the unit cell the repeatable smallest basic structural portion. Despite the engineer wrapper, the stem directly asks for the name of that definition.
NBF p.113 defines differently oriented grains and grain boundaries as polycrystalline structure. The teacher should not equate grain domains with polymer molecules.
entries.compulsoryTeachingClarification: Crystalline domains and polymer macromolecules are distinct concepts

entries.firstPassScienceFinding: NBF p.114 describes short-range ordered pockets amid the lack of long-range repetition in amorphous material. A relevant application of local-versus-long-range distinction.

Original owner Word incorrectly attributes nylon to textbook synthetic examples. V149 entirely rewrites stem/options to a polythene example but preserved the original key position; its original nylon explanation is STILL FALSE and MUST be replaced in a separate teacher-approved keyed source.
NBF p.113 and p.115 connect diffraction to atomic arrangement. Despite experiment framing, the item largely asks recognition of an investigative method and has remote unrelated distractors.
NBF p.113 contrasts a single ordered crystal with differently oriented grains; chemical composition alone does not dictate grain structure. Good comparative application.
NBF Fig.7.5(b) contrasts corner-only SC and corner-plus-body BCC. This is a text-described geometry transformation and duplicates earlier BCC-placement items.

NBF p.113 explicitly links atomic arrangement/bonding to material performance and technological selection. The causal answer is sound; distractors are extremely implausible, weakening Understanding discrimination.
